opus-5.5.text:
For me, meaningful progress isn't really about a single benchmark number going up. Benchmarks are useful, but they saturate quickly, and sometimes a model looks great on paper and then you actually use it and it still feels brittle. So the question I keep asking is: can the model do things that genuinely surprise us, in a good way, things we didn't explicitly train it for?

I think there are a few signals I care about. The first is generalization. When a model learns to reason well in math or code, does that ability actually transfer to messy, open-ended problems in the real world? If capability only shows up inside the narrow distribution you optimized for, that's engineering progress, but it's not really progress toward general intelligence.

The second is the ability to work over long horizons. A lot of real intelligence is not answering one question well; it's planning, trying something, getting feedback, noticing you were wrong, and adjusting, over hours or days. When models can sustain that kind of coherent effort, using tools and interacting with an environment, and not just drift off after a few steps, that feels like a real step.

The third is efficiency, and I think people sometimes underweight it. If we can only get intelligence by throwing ever more compute at the problem, that tells us we haven't fully understood something. When you find a better architecture, a better training recipe, or a better data strategy, and suddenly you get the same capability at a fraction of the cost, that is meaningful, because it means intelligence becomes something many more people can actually access and build on.

And finally, honestly, I think a very simple test is whether it changes how people work. When researchers, engineers, ordinary users start relying on these systems as real collaborators, not toys, and the systems help produce new knowledge rather than just recombining what's already known, that's when I'd say we are clearly moving toward AGI. We're seeing early signs of that, but I think we're still at the beginning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think about this a lot, and my honest answer is that meaningful progress toward AGI doesn't look like a single breakthrough moment. It looks like a few specific capabilities maturing together.

The first is generalization. Right now a model can be remarkably good at tasks that resemble its training distribution and surprisingly fragile outside of it. Real progress means a model that encounters a genuinely new problem, one it has never seen anything like, and can still reason its way through it. Not by pattern matching, but by building an understanding of the problem structure on the fly. That's the difference between memorizing a thousand proofs and actually being able to do mathematics.

The second is what I'd call learning efficiency. Humans learn from very few examples. A child sees a cat twice and understands "cat." We still need enormous amounts of data, and more importantly, we still rely heavily on training-time learning rather than learning during deployment. When a model can continually improve from its own experience, from interacting with the world and correcting its own mistakes, that's a qualitative shift. That's when the loop closes.

The third is reliability in long-horizon tasks. It's one thing to answer a question well. It's another to pursue a goal over hours or days, decompose it, handle unexpected obstacles, know when to back up and try something else, and verify your own work. Agents today can do this for short chains, but the error compounds. Each step you add multiplies the chance of derailing. Getting that compounding error under control is, I think, one of the most practically important milestones, and it's less glamorous than people expect.

And underneath all of this, I'd add something about understanding versus performance. We've become very good at making benchmark numbers go up. But I've seen models score impressively on evaluations and then fail at something a smart undergraduate would find trivial. So part of meaningful progress is also progress in how we measure. If our evaluations can be gamed, we don't actually know where we are.

So when people ask me, "Are we close?" I usually say: look at whether the model can learn something new after training, whether it can work on a hard problem for a long time without falling apart, and whether its capability transfers to things nobody prepared it for. When those three are solidly true, we'll be having a very different conversation. Until then, I think we should be excited but honest about what's been solved and what hasn't.

astra-6.text:
To me, meaningful progress toward AGI means a model can handle something genuinely new—not just a different version of a problem it has already seen. Can it learn from limited experience, recognize when its understanding is incomplete, and revise its approach when it makes a mistake?

I would look beyond whether it gives an impressive answer in one conversation. Can it pursue a goal over many steps, keep track of constraints, and recover when something unexpected happens? And can people reliably understand when to trust it?

So I wouldn’t define progress by a single benchmark. I’d look for broader capability, more efficient learning, and greater reliability developing together. The important question is whether improvements hold up outside the conditions where we measured them.

sol-6.1.text:
To me, meaningful progress toward AGI means that a system can take what it has learned and use it in a genuinely unfamiliar situation. Can it understand a new problem, recognize what information it is missing, and learn from feedback? Can it carry a task through and check whether the result actually makes sense?

I would look beyond performance on any single benchmark. We need to understand how reliably those abilities transfer across tasks, how much guidance the system needs, and whether it recognizes its own limitations. A system that gives an impressive answer once is interesting. A system that consistently solves new problems and corrects its mistakes is a much stronger sign of progress.
